newsitem.title: SPAIN: B/Spain lowers rate, next cut seen in a month.
newsitem.headline: B/Spain lowers rate, next cut seen in a month.

text.p: The Bank of Spain sanctioned its fourth interest rate cut of the year on Friday and analysts said another is just around the corner although it may the last.
The central bank lowered its key money market rate by 25 basis points to 5.25 percent in a widely expected move after a sharp moderation in inflation.
"We think that if inflation stays below two percent in May and the peseta remains stable, they could cut another 25 basis points to five percent," said Heather Richardson, UBS economist.
"We've seen 12 cuts in the last 17 months. I think we'll see 13 in 18 but they can't go on forever."

The rapid-fire easing responds to dramatic drops in Spain's inflation rate. Data on Wednesday showed the consumer price index rose at a modest 1.7 percent year-on-year in April -- its lowest level in nearly 30 years -- from 2.2 percent a month earlier.
Inflation is expected to continue improving this month before rebounding later in the year.
William Thornhill, senior economist at Technical Data, said he saw May CPI moderating to 1.4 or 1.5 percent.
"So they have plenty of room to cut if they wish...If this rate cut had a 90 percent probability, the next cut at mid-June has a 40 percent one," Thornhill said.
While many economists agreed a further rate cut was expected next month, they were divided on whether that would be the last in this cycle given the outlook for an inflation pick-up.
UBS sees inflation ending the year at 2.9 percent, after picking up to 2.5 percent in the fourth quarter. It sees inflation at an average of 2.4 percent in 1997.
As a result, the central bank may decide to quit cutting at five percent, Richardson said.

"We believe the Bank of Spain can cut another 25 basis points to five percent next month after May CPI. Then it will have another 25 basis point scope which it is likely to use in the last quarter of the year, in October of November," said Juan Antonio Mielgo, economist at the Bank of America in Madrid.
